units.title: A Foreigner in Your Own House

grounds.ref: In-depth: What South Africa's power cuts mean for health facilities — Spotlight, 2021
grounds.evidences: Documents that South African hospital operating theatres face real, elevated risk during load-shedding because backup generators are frequently poorly serviced and fail to engage, and that theatre power response must be faster than 0.5 seconds to protect patients mid-procedure.

grounds.ref: Layer of Protection Analysis (LOPA) — Prime Process Safety Center
grounds.evidences: Documents that LOPA exists as a structured, frequency-based method specifically to settle disagreements about whether existing safeguards (such as an alarm) provide enough independent risk reduction or whether a dedicated Safety Instrumented System/trip system rated to a specific SIL is required.

grounds.ref: Preventive maintenance in urban public transport: the role of engine oil analysis — PMC, 2024
grounds.evidences: Shows peer-reviewed evidence that oil condition monitoring (wear metals, contaminants, degradation products) reveals real correlations with developing mechanical failure in vehicle drivetrains/cooling systems, supporting the case that sampling fluid from a sealed housing can reveal internal wear months before an unwarned failure.

grounds.ref: Application of Natural Language Processing for [Aircraft Maintenance Work Order Analysis]. Proceedings, ICAS 2024
grounds.evidences: This paper applies NLP/text-similarity techniques to free-text maintenance technician notes to recover structured failure-mode information that structured fields (often defaulted to catch-all categories like 'Other') fail to capture, directly evidencing that the specific problem of failure information being trapped in unstructured free text rather than countable fields is real and already an active research target in maintenance engineering.

grounds.ref: Reliabilityweb. 'What is Criticality Analysis?' (ISO 14224-referenced asset-criticality consequence ranking)
grounds.evidences: Documents that proper asset criticality ranking is defined as failure frequency multiplied by cost CONSEQUENCE — explicitly including safety, environmental, operational and reputational impact, not just repair/replacement price or acquisition cost — evidencing that ranking a criticality register by asset cost alone is a documented misapplication of the standard method, which is exactly why a cheap asset whose failure consequence stops the whole plant can rank far below its true risk.

grounds.ref: The Cost of Ambiguous Requirements — Victor Font
grounds.evidences: Documents that ambiguous written specifications lead each reader to privately resolve the ambiguity differently, producing incorrect implementations, rework, and cost/schedule overrun once the mismatch surfaces after work has begun.

grounds.ref: Steel Pipe Weld Defect Detection: NDT Methods and Real Failure Case Studies — LongMa
grounds.evidences: States that more than 40% of pipeline/weld failure incidents are rooted in defects that were technically detectable but were missed because of NDT method or coverage limitations — direct evidence that an inspection procedure passing an item does not establish it was capable of finding the flaw that later caused failure.

grounds.ref: Common-Cause Failure Database and Analysis System, NUREG/CR-6268 Rev.1 — U.S. NRC / Idaho National Laboratory
grounds.evidences: Documents that common-cause failures violate the independence assumption underlying simple redundancy math (multiplying two failure probabilities), and provides quantitative beta-factor data showing redundant systems fail together far more often than independence would predict.

grounds.ref: API 579-1/ASME FFS-1: Fitness-For-Service Evaluation for Industry Assets — ASNT
grounds.evidences: Confirms the real, industry-standard gap this unit addresses: new-build pressure vessel codes say nothing about a thinned, damaged, in-service vessel, which is exactly why API 579/ASME FFS-1 was created as the leading standard for judging whether such equipment can continue running.

grounds.ref: White Space Forever — BPMInstitute.org (on Rummler & Brache's 'Improving Performance: How to Manage the White Space on the Organization Chart')
grounds.evidences: Documents that the 'white space' between departments — the unowned handoff points where accountability ends at organizational borders — is where misunderstandings, mistakes and delays occur, matching the unit's claim that process delay hides in the gaps between individually-fast steps rather than in the steps themselves.

grounds.ref: Fatality risk and issues of inequity among vulnerable road users in South Africa — PLOS ONE, 2021
grounds.evidences: Analysing 33,659 fatal crashes (2016-2018), finds pedestrians account for the largest share of road fatalities (39.5%) and up to 38% of national road deaths, with elevated risk on rural/dirt roads — grounding the real, quantified toll of pedestrian road deaths that a toll/fare-based appraisal method values at zero.

grounds.ref: Municipal asset operations and maintenance performance in metropolitan and rural municipalities in Gauteng Province and Vhembe District Local Municipalities, South Africa — Cogent, 2021
grounds.evidences: Peer-reviewed study of South African municipalities finding that condition assessment and asset care practice is present but forward-looking maintenance and renewal planning is weak, i.e. organisations hold condition snapshots without a mechanism to project future network state.

grounds.ref: Infrastructure Paper — Integrated Urban Development Framework, Department of Cooperative Governance (COGTA), South Africa, 2016
grounds.evidences: Official government paper documenting that municipal infrastructure asset portfolios are projected to deteriorate from poor to very poor over coming years under current investment levels, confirming that officials must answer forward-looking questions about network condition, not just report current state.

grounds.ref: Probabilistic Risk Assessment vs worst-case scenario conservatism in engineering safety assessment — literature synthesis (arXiv, robust control / risk analysis)
grounds.evidences: Documents the recognised engineering problem that stacking multiple independent worst-case assumptions into a single deterministic assessment produces unrealistic, excessively conservative (or even misleading) results compared with a probabilistic treatment of the same uncertainties.

grounds.ref: The Bathtub Curve in Reliability Engineering — Tractian, 2024/2025
grounds.evidences: Documents that new fleets pass through an infant-mortality phase with a high but declining failure rate before reaching a stable useful-life phase, and that MTBF is only meaningful in that stable phase — evidencing that a single acceptance-test failure-rate figure can look like it is 'improving' or 'worsening' during this settling period depending on which phase it is read against.

grounds.ref: One-Factor-at-a-Time (OFAT) versus factorial/designed experiments — Curiouscatblog / management literature (Deming-tradition industrial statistics)
grounds.evidences: Confirms that field engineers commonly dispute headline reliability figures using informal day-to-day observation, and that contractual/statistical evaluation of whether new equipment is improving or worsening requires more than a single point-in-time metric — the general problem this unit dramatises.

grounds.ref: Design of Experiments — JMP Statistics Knowledge Portal (SAS Institute)
grounds.evidences: Demonstrates with a worked example that testing multiple suspected causes one at a time can require many more trials than a designed experiment testing all factors together (49 runs vs 12 in the cited case) and can still miss the true optimum because it cannot detect interactions between causes — precisely the fault this unit says the one-at-a-time plan has 'that nobody in the room has mentioned'.

grounds.ref: One-Factor-at-a-Time Versus Designed Experiments — V. Czitrom, The American Statistician, 1999
grounds.evidences: Peer-reviewed statistics literature establishing that OFAT experimentation is both less efficient (needs more runs) and structurally unable to estimate interaction effects between suspected causes, compared with factorial designs that test all suspects within the same limited number of trials.

grounds.ref: Getting Started — Introduction to Systematic Reviews and Other Evidence Synthesis in Engineering, Duke University Libraries
grounds.evidences: Documents the recognised distinction between a systematic review (explicit, reproducible, auditable search/selection method) and an unsystematic narrative review, and the professional expectation that engineering evidence used for major decisions record how sources were found and screened — the exact gap the checker in this unit cannot find a trail for.

grounds.ref: Delusion and Deception in Large Infrastructure Projects: Two Models for Explaining and Preventing Executive Disaster — Flyvbjerg, Garbuio & Lovallo, California Management Review, 2009 (arXiv preprint)
grounds.evidences: Documents that capital-project decision-makers systematically favour optimistic, imprecise low estimates over fully worked, precise (and therefore larger-looking) ones, and that this pattern — not deliberate wrongdoing by any individual in the room — is a well-documented driver of the wrong projects being funded.

grounds.ref: From Nobel Prize to Project Management: getting risks right by reference class forecasting — B. Flyvbjerg (arXiv preprint of Project Management Journal paper)
grounds.evidences: Describes reference class forecasting as a remedy specifically because ordinary committee comparison of a detailed costed proposal against a rough round-number alternative is known to be biased toward the less-developed, cheaper-looking option.

grounds.ref: The real power of real options — McKinsey Quarterly, 1997 (reproduced, Duke University)
grounds.evidences: Establishes that a single static financial calculation (e.g. NPV) has no way to represent the value of waiting for a known future resolution of uncertainty, and that real options analysis exists precisely to price that waiting value — the exact gap the machine-economics decision in this unit is missing.

grounds.ref: Rethinking SAIDI and SAIFI: How Utilities Can Turn Metrics Into Real Reliability Gains — ThinkPower Solutions
grounds.evidences: Directly evidences that a utility's headline average-availability figure (like SAIDI/SAIFI) can be arithmetically correct and still misrepresent what an individual customer actually experienced, because system-wide averages bury pockets of repeated interruptions — the same conflict between a checked-twice percentage and a lived count of twenty stoppages that the unit describes.

grounds.ref: Standby redundancy — in Reliability and Maintenance of Complex Systems, Springer
grounds.evidences: Establishes the standard reliability-engineering framing this unit dramatises: whether to buy one large full-capacity standby spare versus additional units of the ordinary type already in service is a recognised sparing-strategy trade-off with real cost and reliability consequences, not an arbitrary choice.

grounds.ref: Reliability Analysis — JMP Statistics Knowledge Portal (SAS Institute)
grounds.evidences: Directly evidences the unit's core failure: shows with a worked example that excluding still-running (censored/suspended) units from a failure-time calculation biases the estimated failure probability upward — in the cited example from about 2% to 10% — which is exactly what happens when an MTBF figure is computed only from items that have already broken.

grounds.ref: Reforming Sustainability-Linked Bonds by Strengthening Investor Trust — Journal of Risk and Financial Management, MDPI, 2024
grounds.evidences: Peer-reviewed finance research documenting that sustainability-linked instruments routinely include KPIs that lack standardised, verifiable measurement methods, and that this gap is a recognised driver of greenwashing risk — evidencing the unit's scenario of a lender wanting to sign for a target that 'there is no measure of, and there never has been'.

grounds.ref: The Influence of Porosity on Fatigue Crack Initiation in Additively Manufactured Titanium Components — Scientific Reports, Nature, 2017
grounds.evidences: Peer-reviewed evidence that two nominally identical parts made of the same material, under the same nominal stress, can have very different fatigue lives because of small, unrecorded variations in internal defects (porosity/inclusions) invisible to a standard stress calculation — grounding the unit's two brackets that crack at different times despite identical sign-off calculations.

grounds.ref: Paris' law (Paris–Erdogan crack growth equation) — Wikipedia, summarising the established fracture-mechanics model
grounds.evidences: Confirms the physical basis of the unit's central claim: fatigue crack growth rate da/dN is a function of stress intensity, which itself increases with crack size, so growth accelerates as the crack gets bigger — meaning the time already taken to reach the current 6mm size is not a linear guide to the time remaining before the plate fails.

units.title: t-drum-buffer-rope

grounds.evidences: Documents that in a system with an identified constraint, overall throughput is set by that one constraint, and that without deliberately pacing and buffering work to it (the drum-buffer-rope mechanism this unit is about), teams can be fully busy while output and on-time delivery still swing between overload and starvation.

units.title: t-focusing-steps

grounds.ref: Theory of Constraints (TOC): The Manufacturing Guide — Fabrico
grounds.evidences: Documents the core TOC finding that at any moment a system has exactly one binding constraint, and that effort spent improving non-constraint steps yields no increase in overall throughput — directly evidencing the unit's premise that a flat-out, hard-working team can still see the mission-level number barely move because effort is aimed at the wrong point.

units.title: t-MOBILISE-ASSETS

grounds.ref: South Africa — Growth Lab, Harvard Kennedy School
grounds.evidences: States that South Africa's underlying capabilities — its people, companies, assets and know-how — remain underutilised relative to what is needed for sustained growth, evidencing the unit's claim that people surrounded by idle value nonetheless perceive themselves as having 'nothing'.

grounds.ref: GEM South Africa 2022/2023 report — Global Entrepreneurship Monitor / Stellenbosch Business School
grounds.evidences: Documents that up to 80% of South African MSMEs are excluded from formal lending by high collateral demands, forcing would-be entrepreneurs to work with whatever informal assets, skills, space and trust they already hold rather than capital they cannot access — the real-world condition behind the unit's premise.

units.title: t-ORIGINATE-THE-DEAL

grounds.ref: Buyer power provisions under South Africa's competition law — ENSafrica, 2020
grounds.evidences: Confirms that unequal negotiating power between small suppliers and large dominant buyers is a recognised, regulated problem in South Africa (Competition Act s.8(4), 2019 amendment and the 2020 Buyer Power Regulations), grounding the unit's premise that a small player asking a much bigger one for a fair deal faces a real structural disadvantage.

units.title: t-throughput

grounds.evidences: Documents, with concrete case examples (including an aerospace supplier and a vehicle-painting operation), how a cost-accounting-driven saving that looks obviously smart on a spreadsheet can increase inventory, create bottleneck starvation, or trigger costly overtime elsewhere — quietly making the whole operation harder even though the isolated saving is real.
